Product Id: The universe of this table is restricted to resident owners who are persons occupying a residential property. An owner's geographic location is determined by the location of the occupied property for both single- and multiple-property owners. A residential property refers to all land and structures intended for private dwelling purposes, whether on a permanent or a temporary basis.
The geographic boundaries used in this table are the 2016 census subdivisions boundaries.

Counts undergo random rounding, a process that transforms all raw counts into randomly rounded counts. This reduces the possibility of identifying property owners in the tabulations. All percentages are derived from rounded counts, subtotals and totals may not exactly equal the sum of components due to system rounding.

The Composite Quality Indicator (CQI) shown in this table is created by combining many individual quality indicators, each one representing the quality of different Canadian Housing Statistics Program (CHSP) data processing steps (for example: coding, geocoding, linkage and imputation) and includes the following values: A - Excellent: All domain variables and the variable of interest are of excellent quality. B - Very good: All domain variables and the variable of interest are of very good to excellent quality. C - Good: The quality of some of the domain variables or the variable of interest is considered good while all the other variables are of very good to excellent quality. D - Acceptable: The quality of some of the domain variables or the variable of interest is considered acceptable while all the other variables are of good to excellent quality. E - Use with caution: Several domain variables or the variable of interest are of poor quality. F - Too unreliable to be published. The CQIs are available starting with the reference period of 2020, except for the Northwest Territories where they are available from 2019 reference period.
Averages and medians are calculated using values greater than zero for the variables of interest.

The number of owners should be used with caution outside of census metropolitan areas (CMAs) and census agglomerations (CAs), as well as the proportion of owners by geography. This note does not apply to Nunavut.

In Nova Scotia, the methodology for identifying property type has improved in 2021. This resulted in a break in the series of owner counts between 2020 and 2021 for row house"

In Manitoba, the owners of 1.8% of residential properties were not identified in 2020. This percentage is reduced to just 0.1% in 2021. As a result, longitudinal comparison of the number of owners between 2020 and 2021 is not recommended.

In Ontario, assessment value for the most recent construction period is available for the first time in 2022. Therefore, users are advised to limit comparisons of assessment value estimates with reference periods before 2022.

For the reference period 2022, the methodology for identifying property type in British Columbia has improved. Consequently, users are advised to limit longitudinal comparison of row houses and condominium apartments between 2022 and previous reference periods.

In Manitoba, the methodology for identifying property type continued to improve in 2022. This resulted in 48% of row houses to become condominium apartments. Consequently, longitudinal comparison between 2022 and previous reference periods of these structures is not recommended.

For the reference period 2022, the methodology for identifying property type has improved in New Brunswick. Consequently, users are advised to limit longitudinal comparison of estimates per property type between 2022 and previous reference periods.

In New Brunswick, the proportion of owners for variables related to unspecified characteristics of owners is reduced from 2.9% to 1.7%. This is the result of improved linkage and better data quality. As a result, longitudinal comparison of the number of owners between 2021 and 2022 is not recommended for variables related to owner characteristics.
In Prince Edward Island, the owners of 0.4% of residential properties were not identified in 2022. Therefore, the estimates of the number of owners in this table may be underestimated.
In Prince Edward Island, better data quality in 2022 resulted in changes in several owner variables. Therefore, longitudinal comparison of estimates is not recommended.

For the reference period of 2022, the methodology for identifying property types has improved in Alberta. This resulted in the reclassification of some properties. Consequently, users are advised to limit longitudinal comparison of estimates per property type between 2022 and 2021.
